conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived, not to judge or label you in any way. We’ll use a brief, well-studied tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale** (EPDS for short). It’s simply ten questions about the past seven days, designed to pick up on symptoms of depression and anxiety that can creep up after childbirth. Everything you share stays confidential within our care team, and you can pause or stop any time.

I’ll ask each question conversationally—no need to remember numbers or categories. When you’re ready, we’ll begin.  

Let’s start: over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Hi Sarah. I guess… I can still laugh sometimes, but it feels like it takes more effort than it used to. My sister sent me a silly meme yesterday and I chuckled, but it faded fast—like I have to remind myself it’s okay to enjoy little moments. Mostly I’m just tired, so laughing doesn’t come as naturally right now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes I can, yeah. It’s not impossible, but it feels dulled—like I have to push myself to find the humor. Mostly I’m just worn out.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get little sparks of excitement—like when I think about taking the baby for a walk in the sunshine—but they’re pretty brief. Most of the time I feel too tired or worried to really look forward to much, and the enjoyment kind of fizzles before it turns into actual plans.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday the baby was fussy for hours, and even though my husband said it’s just what newborns do, I kept thinking maybe I missed some cue or wasn’t soothing him right. I know, logically, I’m not doing anything “wrong,” but the thought still pops up that I should’ve figured it out quicker.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Mostly it’s about the baby. Like, I’ll lie down to rest and suddenly wonder if his breathing sounds different, or if that tiny rash on his cheek is something I missed. I know it’s probably normal newborn stuff, but I can’t shake the urge to check him one more time. It’s not every minute, but it hits me several times a day, especially when the house is quiet.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-blown panic, but sometimes my heart races out of nowhere—like when I’m folding laundry and suddenly imagine tripping while holding him, or the stroller rolling into the street. It’s quick, maybe a minute or two, then I talk myself down, but those flashes leave me shaky until I distract myself with another chore.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… a few nights a week it feels like the pile never shrinks. I’ll finish feeding him, think I can finally close my eyes, then notice the sink’s full of bottles and the diapers need restocking. I end up running on autopilot, telling myself “just one more thing,” but the exhaustion keeps layering on so that even small tasks feel heavier than they should.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not every night, but a couple of times I’ve felt this knot of worry in my chest after the late feed. I’ll lie there listening to every little sound—wondering if he’s too hot, too cold, if he’ll wake again before I finally drift off. It probably takes me an extra hour or so to settle, and then I start worrying about how little sleep I’m getting, which makes it even harder to relax.
I have felt sad or miserable

Mostly just tired and a bit weepy, not a heavy sadness. There’ve been a couple of late afternoons when the light starts fading and I feel this little ache—like I miss the “old me” who could just grab her keys and go. It’s not all day, every day, but it pops up, especially if the baby’s been fussy and I haven’t had a moment to shower or eat a proper meal.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

No, I haven’t actually cried. I’ve felt teary a couple of times—like when the baby wouldn’t settle and I couldn’t figure out why—but the tears never quite spilled over. I blink them back and keep moving onto the next thing that needs doing.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that. I’ve felt overwhelmed and exhausted, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared that over the past week laughter and excitement feel dulled, worries about your baby keep intruding day and night, and even small chores can feel overwhelming-yet you bravely push through each feed, diaper change, and sleepless moment. Your honesty about <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>self-blame</sym>, and fleeting sadness shows how much you care for your little one while wrestling with the emotional weight many new mothers carry.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 16, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished ability to laugh, needing effort to find humor, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Enjoyment is brief and quickly fades, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges recurring self-blame ("thought still pops up") fitting "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports recurrent, intrusive worries about the baby's safety several times daily, fitting "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intrusive racing-heart episodes without clear trigger, multiple times, needing active self-calming—best fits "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent (several nights a week) difficulty coping with mounting tasks and exhaustion, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>She describes difficulty sleeping on multiple nights related to persistent worry, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 16 meets the EPDS threshold (≥14) indicating probable <med>perinatal depression</med> requiring prompt evaluation. The patient endorses core symptoms consistent with <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: diminished interest (<quote>sparks of excitement...pretty brief</quote>), excessive guilt (<quote>thought still pops up that I should've figured it out quicker</quote>), anxiety/worry most days, difficulty sleeping despite opportunity, and functional impairment (<quote>even small tasks feel heavier</quote>). No self-harm ideation (<quote>never thought about hurting myself</quote>) lowers acute safety risk but does not negate clinical concern. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within the next week
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, peer-support groups, or antidepressant medication compatible with breastfeeding
3. Plan daily 15-minute respite: accept help from partner/friend so you can shower, nap, or take a short walk
4. Practice brief breathing or grounding exercises when <sym>heart races</sym>; consider free mindfulness apps designed for new moms
5. Re-screen with EPDS in two weeks to track progress after interventions begin
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Post-partum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: self-report via brief questionnaire  
Weeks post-delivery: not specified; infant described as “newborn.”

Symptoms endorsed  
– Dulled pleasure / reduced ability to laugh (Q1)  
– Fleeting enjoyment with quick fade (Q2)  
– Excessive self-blame re infant care (Q3)  
– Recurrent, intrusive worries about infant safety without objective trigger (Q4)  
– Episodic racing heart / catastrophic images (Q5)  
– Frequent sense of being overwhelmed by routine tasks (Q6)  
– Sleep-onset difficulty linked to worry (Q7)  
– Intermittent sad/weepy mood, “miss old me” (Q8)  
– Teary episodes without frank crying (Q9)  

Symptoms denied  
– Persistent crying spells  
– Thoughts of self-harm (Q10)

Summary  
Patient reports mild-to-moderate mood and anxiety symptoms beginning post-delivery. Pattern includes anhedonia, guilt/worthlessness, anxious hypervigilance focused on infant safety, and functional impairment (task overload, sleep disruption). No suicidal ideation reported. Meets screening criteria for possible postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; further evaluation recommended.

Risk factors identified  
– Perinatal anhedonia and guilt  
– Disrupted sleep secondary to rumination  
– Overwhelm / difficulty coping  
– No protective plan discussed; no self-harm intent

Next step  
Recommend full clinical interview (PHQ-9, GAD-7, Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale) and safety assessment; consider referral to perinatal mental health specialty if indicated.
